notes.meaning: The young woman wishes her beloved were like a baby brother who nursed at her mother's breasts. In her culture, lovers could not show affection in the streets without causing a scandal, but family members could openly kiss. She longs to show her deep love for him anywhere without being judged or looked down upon.

She imagines bringing her beloved into her childhood home, the place where her mother raised and guided her. There she wants to honor him by offering him her very best spiced wine and fresh pomegranate juice. This shows her desire to bring him into her closest family circle and share all her finest treasures with him.

The bride describes resting peacefully in the embrace of her husband. His left hand supports her head while his right hand holds her close. This picture expresses the tender protection, closeness, and security they share in their marriage.

The young woman speaks again to the young women of Jerusalem, urging them not to rush romantic passion. True marital love is sacred and must not be forced before its proper time. It should be allowed to wait until both hearts and circumstances are ready for it.

Onlookers marvel as the bride comes up from the open countryside, leaning all her weight on her beloved. She speaks of awakening his love under an apple tree, near the place where his mother brought him into the world. It shows how fully she relies on his strength and cherishes the humble beginnings of their relationship.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Older Latin interpreters read this verse allegorically, seeing the apple tree as the cross of Christ and the mother in labor as the old covenant synagogue.

notes.meaning: The bride asks to be kept like an engraved seal upon her beloved's heart and arm. In ancient times, a personal seal marked precious ownership that was never given away. She asks for an exclusive and lasting bond, because true marital love is as strong and unyielding as death itself.

No flood of rushing water can put out true love, and no wealth can purchase it. If a wealthy man tried to trade his entire estate to buy someone's affection, his offer would be completely laughed at. Genuine love is a willing gift of the heart that money can never buy.

The family recalls their younger sister from the days before she was old enough for courtship. Under ancient custom, older brothers were responsible for protecting a sister's honor and future. They discuss how they will care for her when a suitor finally comes to ask for her hand in marriage.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view verses 8 through 14 as a later epilogue or separate collection of songs attached to the close of the book.

notes.meaning: The brothers decide how they will guide their sister based on her choices. If she stands firm like a wall by keeping her moral purity, they will honor and protect her like a shining silver tower. But if she is like an open door, swinging wide to every temptation, they will guard her strictly behind heavy cedar boards.

The bride declares that she guarded her purity like a solid wall before she married. Now that she is grown, she brings honor, defense, and beauty to her marriage. Because of her faithfulness, she found favor and peace in the eyes of her husband.

Solomon owned a huge, valuable vineyard at Baal-hamon that he leased out to tenant farmers. Each worker was required to bring in one thousand pieces of silver for its harvest. This highlights the king's vast wealth and his commercial business dealings.

The bride explains that her own vineyard, representing her body and her love, belongs to her to give as she pleases. Solomon is welcome to his great financial profit and his hired workers may keep their wages. Unlike a rented field, her devotion is given freely to her husband and cannot be bought or sold.

The bridegroom addresses his wife while she lingers in the gardens with her companions. Her friends are listening to her speak, but he eagerly asks to hear her voice himself. He desires her sweet words and attention above everyone else around her.

The song closes with the bride calling her beloved to run swiftly to her like a young gazelle across spice-covered hills. Their joy and romantic excitement remain just as vibrant as when they first fell in love. Even at the end, their relationship is full of energetic longing and eager delight.
